short: Seventy years of soldier-emperors between the Tang and the Song.
full:
When Zhu Wen ended the Tang in 907 he founded the first of five short-lived dynasties that held the Yellow River plain in succession: Later Liang, Later Tang, Later Jin, Later Han and Later Zhou. None lasted more than seventeen years, and most ended when a general took the throne from a child. In the south and west, where the fighting was lighter, ten more durable kingdoms formed, among them Wu-Yue around Hangzhou and Southern Tang at Nanjing, which sheltered scholars and trade while the north tore itself apart.

One decision outlasted the period. In 938 the founder of the Later Jin, who owed his throne to Khitan help, ceded the Sixteen Prefectures around modern Beijing to the Liao. That handed the steppe the passes through the northern mountains, and no later Chinese dynasty recovered them until the Ming. In 960 the Later Zhou commander Zhao Kuangyin was proclaimed emperor by his own troops at Chenqiao and founded the Song, which absorbed the southern kingdoms one by one and took the last of them in 979.
